sections.heading: 3.2.2. Node Input Packing: Summary, Evidence, Parent Results, Subtask
sections.text: Each node v v is formatted as a standalone task instance with four fields: a compact summary s ⁡ ( v ) s(v) , planner-provided evidence e ⁡ ( v ) e(v) , parent results r ⁡ ( pa ⁡ ( v ) ) r(\mathrm{pa}(v)) , and the subtask content c ⁡ ( v ) c(v) : (5) inp ⁡ ( v ) = Template ⁡ ( s ⁡ ( v ) , e ⁡ ( v ) , r ⁡ ( pa ⁡ ( v ) ) , c ⁡ ( v ) ) . \mathrm{inp}(v)=\mathrm{Template}\big(s(v),\,e(v),\,r(\mathrm{pa}(v)),\,c(v)\big). The summary carries global or branch context without repeatedly inserting the full question, evidence captures local constraints, and parent results pass intermediate outputs.

sections.heading: 3.2.3. Root Initialization, Branch Summaries, and Global Synthesis
sections.text: The root calls Decompose once to initialize the graph, producing K ∈ [ 1 , 5 ] K\in[1,5] subtasks and a root summary s root s_{\text{root}} that all first-layer nodes inherit. When a non-root node takes Decompose , the large model generates child subtasks and a branch summary s branch s_{\text{branch}} , which downstream nodes inherit to keep context compact and branch-specific. Execution ends when all leaves are solved or expansion stops under budget or depth limits, after which a large model performs a single global synthesis over the available node results to produce y ^ ​ ( x ) \hat{y}(x) . If some queued nodes remain unsolved due to budget exhaustion, we include an explicit UNSOLVED_DUE_TO_BUDGET marker in the synthesis input so the model does not implicitly invent missing results.

sections.heading: 3.3. Training Data and Supervision
sections.text: RouteGoT does not require node-level ground-truth labels for intermediate subtasks at inference time. Instead, we train the router offline using a three-strategy contrast pool constructed from standard task datasets with reference answers. For each training instance u u (a standalone task with a ground-truth answer), we run all three strategies a ∈ { IO , CoT , Decompose } a\in\{\textsf{IO},\textsf{CoT},\textsf{Decompose}\} and log (i) correctness y a ​ ( u ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } y_{a}(u)\in\{0,1\} by matching the strategy output against the ground truth and (ii) the realized token cost c a ​ ( u ) ∈ ℝ + c_{a}(u)\in\mathbb{R}^{+} from execution traces. At inference time, we format every graph node as a task instance inp ⁡ ( v ) \mathrm{inp}(v) and apply the same router to both the root and intermediate subtask nodes. Cost definition. For IO and CoT , c a ​ ( u ) c_{a}(u) is the total tokens of a single model call (input+output). For Decompose , which triggers a graph reasoning procedure, we define cost as the total tokens accumulated over the entire graph run: (6) c Decompose ​ ( u ) = ∑ call ∈ GraphRuns ​ ( u ) tokens ⁡ ( call ) . c_{\textsf{Decompose}}(u)=\sum_{\text{call}\in\text{GraphRuns}(u)}\mathrm{tokens}(\text{call}). All-fail handling. Instances with y IO ​ ( u ) = y CoT ​ ( u ) = y Decompose ​ ( u ) = 0 y_{\textsf{IO}}(u)=y_{\textsf{CoT}}(u)=y_{\textsf{Decompose}}(u)=0 are treated as all-fail and excluded when fitting budget thresholds to reduce skew from outliers.

sections.heading: 4.1.1. Datasets
sections.text: We use (i) a heterogeneous pool to train the routing components, and (ii) a set of challenging benchmarks to evaluate end-to-end performance. Router Training Pool. To train the learned components of RouteGoT, we build a heterogeneous dataset of 20,000 instances drawn from 12 reasoning and QA benchmarks (Table 1 ). Each instance is a standalone task with a reference answer. We run three strategies, IO , CoT , and Decompose , and record (i) correctness y a ​ ( u ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } y_{a}(u)\in\{0,1\} and (ii) realized token cost c a ​ ( u ) c_{a}(u) (input + output tokens) for each action a a . These logs supervise success prediction, budget construction via required-cost percentiles, and policy learning through budget-feasible soft targets that trade off correctness against inverse cost, with full details in Appendix B . We evaluate RouteGoT across three task categories. For advanced reasoning , we use GPQA (Diamond split) ( Rein et al., 2024 ) , evaluating all 198 questions with shuffled options to reduce position bias. For retrieval & multi-hop QA , we use HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) , MoreHopQA ( Schnitzler et al., 2024 ) , and HybridQA ( Chen et al., 2020 ) . To control cost, we randomly sample 100 instances from each benchmark with a fixed seed. We use the dataset-provided context (passages/tables) and do not perform external web retrieval; the exact input formatting is provided in Appendix B . For explorative reasoning , we include Game of 24 and Crosswords , following the standard test splits and evaluation protocol from the original ToT setup ( Yao et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: 4.1.4. Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: For multiple-choice GPQA, we report exact-match accuracy on the chosen option after shuffling the answer choices. For open-ended QA and reasoning benchmarks, we evaluate semantic equivalence with a Qwen3-30B judge: given a prediction y ^ \hat{y} and reference y y , the judge returns a binary correctness label (see Appendix D for the prompt). The judge is blind to method identity and uses deterministic decoding. For explorative reasoning tasks, we follow the evaluation protocol from ToT ( Yao et al., 2023 ) . We report average input and output tokens per query and ouput tokens are computed as the sum over all model calls during reasoning, including planning, node execution, synthesis, and router overhead when applicable. sections.heading: B.1. Router Training Pool Configuration
sections.text: The training pool consists of 20,000 instances sampled from 12 reasoning benchmarks to ensure that the learned router generalizes across various patterns, including mathematical logic and multi-hop retrieval. For offline data collection, we maintain consistency with our evaluation by employing Qwen3-4B as the small model for Direct actions, Qwen3-8B as the medium model for CoT , and Qwen3-30B as the large model for the Decompose action. The compute tiers are derived from the empirical distribution of the required cost c req ​ ( u ) c_{\text{req}}(u) , defined as the minimum cost among all successful actions. Based on the training logs, the 25th percentile ( B 25 B_{25} ) is 185 tokens and the 75th percentile ( B 75 B_{75} ) is 1,186 tokens. These define our three-tier difficulty classification used by the PolicyNet to mask actions exceeding the predicted tier’s budget cap.

sections.heading: C.1. Hardware Infrastructure and Serving
sections.text: Experiments were conducted on a GPU cluster equipped with four NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48GB) units. The Qwen3 model family was deployed using the vLLM serving engine to support multi-tier reasoning. To optimize memory usage and throughput, the 30B model was served across two GPUs via tensor parallelism, while the 8B and 4B models were each assigned to a single GPU. This configuration ensures that all heterogeneous experts remain resident in memory, allowing for a realistic assessment of latency and cost-accuracy trade-offs.

sections.heading: C.4. Online Execution and Baselines
sections.text: To ensure stability during inference, RouteGoT uses fixed cost estimates for budget-aware scheduling. For the RouteLLM baseline, we configured binary selection logic between IO (Weak) and Decompose (Strong) actions with a decision threshold of 0.5.
